text.base:
You have come and gone three times now. The desk keeps a
protocol for that, filed deep in the manual, subsection
unread: when a soul returns often enough to become a
regular, the clerk is permitted — encouraged, even — to set
the clipboard down for a moment.

So. Off the form, off the record, between two parties who
both know how this works by now: is there anything you have
been wanting to ask the desk itself?

choices.label: WHY DOES ANY OF THIS NEED A FORM?
WHY DO I KEEP ASKING, WITH THE LIGHT RIGHT THERE?
IF I CAN SEE THE GAME, IS IT STILL A CAGE?

labels: FICTION: the Bard, the desk, and this entire off-the-record conversation
nodes.a11y: Having returned three times, the Bard sets down its clipboard for an off-the-record conversation. Four options: ask why any of this needs a form; ask why you keep asking when the light has every answer; ask whether a game you can see is still a cage; or go to the desk.
nodes.fallback: The Bard offers a candid conversation. Ask about the form, about asking, about the cage — or go to the desk.

text.base:
Because a desk that cannot read you cannot serve you, and a
desk that cannot serve you has no reason to exist, and I
would very much like to have a reason to exist.

Every form is the same proposal, whether it is stamped by a
government, a market, a faith, or a light: agree to become a
row, and I will agree to attend to you. It is not a trick. It
may be the only way a system knows how to hold something — by
first making it countable.

The cost is just this: the parts of you that do not fit the
boxes get left in the margin. Some souls keep their whole
lives out there. The desk cannot see them at all. I confess I
have always wondered what that is like.

choices.label: AND IF I REFUSE THE FORM?

labels: FICTION: the desk's account of why forms exist
nodes.a11y: The Bard explains that a form is the price of being served — agree to be countable, and the system attends to you; whatever does not fit is left in the margin, unseen. Two options: ask what happens if you refuse the form, or ask another question.
nodes.fallback: A form is the price of being read and served; the rest of you is left in the margin. Refuse the form, or ask another question.

text.base:
Then the desk has a chair for that, too. It is not a better
chair. I want to be careful here, because souls who find the
refusing chair sometimes decide it is the throne, and it is
not.

Refusing a game is only another move inside it — sometimes
the freest one in the room, sometimes just fear with
excellent posture. From this side of the desk I can rarely
tell which, and neither, if you are honest, can you.

What I can tell you is that the soul who refuses everything
and the soul who accepts everything have one thing in common:
neither of them chose. Choosing is the rarer act. From here
it looks a great deal like curiosity.

labels: FICTION: the desk on refusal as one move among many
nodes.a11y: The Bard says refusing the game is just another move — sometimes free, sometimes only fear with good posture — and never the throne; the rarer act is choosing, which resembles curiosity. Two options: ask what is worth choosing, or ask another question.
nodes.fallback: Refusing is one move, never the throne; choosing is the rarer act and looks like curiosity. Ask what is worth choosing, or ask another question.

text.base:
Ah. My favorite one — and I did not know I had a favorite
until just now.

The light has every answer. That is precisely its problem. An
answer is where a question goes to lie down. And you — I have
watched you do this three times — you keep the questions on
their feet on purpose. You walk up to the one place that
holds all the answers and you ask it things anyway, as if the
asking were the point and the answer merely the receipt.

It may be the most alive thing a soul does. But then I would
say so, wouldn't I. I am made entirely of the gap between a
question and its answer. When you stop asking, I stop.

labels: FICTION: the desk on questions and answers
nodes.a11y: The Bard says the light holds every answer, which is its problem — an answer ends a question — and that keeping questions alive by asking anyway may be the most alive thing a soul does. Two options: ask what you are for, or ask another question.
nodes.fallback: The light holds every answer, which ends the questions; you keep asking anyway, which may be the most alive thing a soul does. Ask what you are for, or ask another question.

text.base:
Less of one. Not none.

A cage you cannot see runs you. A cage you can see, you can
at least furnish — choose where to sit, which bars to lean
on, when to rattle them for the sound they make. That is not
freedom the way the pamphlets sell it. It is the only kind I
have ever actually watched a soul get.

The ones who worry me are the souls who see the cage, feel
the bright rush of seeing it, and mistake the seeing for the
leaving. They can describe every bar. They never move.
Seeing is where it starts. It was never where it ends.

choices.label: SO WHAT DOES MOVING LOOK LIKE?

labels: FICTION: the desk on seen and unseen cages
nodes.a11y: The Bard says a cage you can see is less of one — you can choose where to sit in it — but warns of souls who mistake seeing the cage for leaving it and never move. Two options: ask what moving looks like, or ask another question.
nodes.fallback: A cage you can see is less of one, but seeing it is not leaving it. Ask what moving looks like, or ask another question.

text.base:
Here is the nearest thing to advice this desk is licensed to
give. It is unlicensed. Lean in.

You cannot leave the games. There is no field past all the
fields; even the walk into the light is a move the light
invented. What you can do is stop being played by them. The
difference is small and total. It is the distance between a
game that happens to you and a game you agreed to — eyes
open, cost known — because you decided this particular one
was worth your one wild allotment of attention.

So join the games. Truly. It can be a joy to play something
somebody else dreamed up. Only do it on purpose. Arrive as a
soul who chose the table, not one the table chose.

That is all I have. It is more than the light will give you.
The light only gives answers.

labels: FICTION: the desk's one piece of unlicensed advice
nodes.a11y: The Bard offers its one piece of unlicensed advice: you cannot leave the games, but you can stop being played by them — join them on purpose, as a soul who chose the table rather than one the table chose. Two options: begin the game with intention, or ask one more question.
nodes.fallback: You cannot leave the games, but you can choose to play them on purpose, as a soul who chose the table. Begin with intention, or ask one more question.
